learning_outcomes.text: Relate the theory of signals and systems within the algebraic theory of signal spaces and operator spaces.
Apply general theory to both traditional system analysis and mathematical modeling of physical problems.
Manage the general concept of transformation and frame the particular transformations addressed in the course within this concept.

Relate - establishing similarities and differences - discrete and continuous variable signal spaces with their associated usual algebra, as well as work with signal parameters associated with each signal space.

Understand the particularization of general algebraic analysis to the case of continuous variable signals and systems, comprehending the need to introduce mathematical concepts associated with these spaces such as the theory of distributions or generalized functions.

Understand, apply and operate the theory of signals and systems in continuous variable: theory of distributions, Fourier series expansion, Fourier transform and Laplace transform seen as particular cases of the general definition of transformation, as well as the spectral analysis of systems associated with these transformations, including simple examples of circuit analysis, modulations, filtering, etc.

Understand, apply and operate the theory of signals and systems in discrete variable: Fourier series expansion, Fourier transform and Z-transform seen as particular cases of the general definition of transformation, as well as the spectral analysis of systems associated with these transformations, including simple examples of discrete systems.
Be able to operate in both continuous and discrete variables, understanding the relationship between both signal spaces.

Be able to apply the concepts of ideal signal sampling to relate both continuous and discrete variable signals and systems, as well as the transformed domains previously analyzed in continuous and discrete variables, and design simple continuous systems in terms of discrete systems.

syllabus_topics: Relationship between algebra/calculus and signal and system theory
Review of vector spaces and particularization of signal spaces
Definition of Dirac delta and physical meaning
Relationship of Dirac delta with step function
Operations with distributions (derivatives, convolutions, product and system resolution)
Relationship of DSF with linear and invariant systems
Relationship between TF and linear and invariant systems
Spectral energy and power density for deterministic signals
Periodic signals: Fourier series expansion (DSF) of discrete signals
Definition of DSF for discrete variable signals
Convergence of DSF for discrete variable signals
Properties of DSF for discrete variable signals
Examples of DSF for discrete variable signals
Relationship of DSF with linear and invariant systems
Aperiodic signals: Fourier transform (TF) of discrete signals
Definition of TF for discrete variable signals
Convergence of TF for discrete variable signals
Properties of TF for discrete variable signals
Examples of TF for discrete variable signals
Relationship of TF with linear and invariant systems
Continuous and discrete variable signals and systems
Sampling and reconstruction of continuous variable signals
Modeling a continuous LTI system using a discrete LTI system
assessment_rules: For the ordinary call, the final theoretical block grade (BT) is the exam grade (EXO). The final classroom practice grade (BPA) is min(10, PAE + 0.3xCPAE). The final laboratory practice grade (BPL) is 0.35x(0.8xP1 + 0.2T1) + 0.65x(0.8xP2 + 0.2xT2). The final grade is calculated as 0.7xBT + 0.1xBPA + 0.2xBPL. For the extraordinary call, there is a single theoretical exam (EXE), an classroom practice exam (EPA), and a laboratory practice exam (EPL). By default, the BPA and BPL grades from the ordinary call are kept, unless the student takes the EPA or EPL, respectively. The final grade is 0.7xEXE + 0.1xEPA + 0.2xEPL. No grades from previous courses are considered, and grades from the current course are not saved for subsequent courses.
